acquisition.why: Inbound works: SEO for 'luxury toilet hire Kent/London', wedding directories like Hitched and Bridebook, and venue/planner partnerships. Partnerships need a human relationship at the start.

onboarding.why: Agents can run the quote, availability calendar, contract and deposit. Site access and pitch checks need some human confirmation.

delivery.why: Physical work every event: towing (B+E licence), setup, servicing, cleaning and waste disposal. A human is needed each time.

billing.why: Deposits and per-event invoices fit standard Stripe/Xero automation.

support.why: Event-day problems (blockages, water, power) need a human on call at weekends.

scores.R_why: A UK trailer costs about £20-40k [E], far beyond the £300 test budget. Weekend event delivery and cleaning conflicts with 6-8 h/week and a toddler. It also needs a waste carrier registration and a tow vehicle.
scores.M_why: An established, crowded UK niche with many local operators. Demand is seasonal (May-Sep). AI does not threaten it, but competition on price and quality is local and physical.
scores.one_line: Physical, capital-heavy weekend logistics with second-hand, promotional US figures. It cannot be agent-run and is far beyond a £300 budget.

acquisition.why: SEO, content, comparison sites and an accountant/app marketplace (Xero/HMRC software list) are inbound. The market is crowded, so paid ads would be expensive.

onboarding.why: Self-serve signup and an Open Banking connection flow (via an aggregator such as TrueLayer).

delivery.why: Unattended SaaS once built. Building a reliable MTD-compliant product needs significant engineering and correctness checks.

support.why: Financial-data and tax questions carry high stakes and liability. Human escalation would be frequent.

scores.R_why: Ricardo is technical, but a UK bookkeeping product needs HMRC MTD recognition, Open Banking aggregator costs, GDPR/security work and accounting accuracy. That is not feasible at 6-8 h/week on £300. A landing-page waitlist test is feasible.
scores.M_why: Xero, QuickBooks, FreeAgent (free with some banks), plus Coconut, Pandle and others crowd the UK market. Bank apps and AI assistants are commoditising basic P&L. Switching costs favour incumbents.
scores.one_line: Saturated, regulated UK market. The only first-hand evidence is a hypothetical price and a domain purchase, with no customers. A poor fit despite being software.

acquisition.why: It depends entirely on an existing podcast audience, which Ricardo does not have. Cold app-store discovery for a generic story app is weak.

onboarding.why: App-store install and signup are self-serve.

delivery.why: Audio playback is software. Story content creation needs a creator.

support.why: The community needs moderation, especially with sensitive personal sharing. Agents can triage, but a human must decide escalations.

scores.R_why: The idea is a companion app for an established show (Nothing Much Happens). Without a comparable audience or IP, Ricardo would face a cold start. Community moderation also creates UK Online Safety Act duties.
scores.M_why: Calm, Headspace, Spotify and AI-generated sleep-story apps saturate the space. Its value is tied to one creator's IP.
scores.one_line: A creator-IP-dependent app with no revenue data and only one source. It cannot be replicated without an audience.

acquisition.why: App Store search/ASO is inbound but platform-dependent, and the category is crowded.

support.why: Low-touch; agents can handle FAQs and reviews.

scores.R_why: Ricardo has the skills. The £79/yr Apple developer fee fits the budget, and the app is buildable in a few weekends. The weakness is distribution and differentiation, not feasibility.
scores.M_why: Dozens of teleprompter apps exist (PromptSmart, BIGVU, Teleprompter Premium), many free. CapCut/iOS features and AI-generated clones commoditise them. The source itself shows it can be built for 2 cents.
scores.one_line: Highly automatable and cheap to test, but the source shows a 2-cent personal clone, not a business. Headroom in a free-clone-saturated App Store category is minimal.

acquisition.why: Inbound via SEO ('finish my Lovable app'), Upwork/Fiverr and Lovable/Replit community expert listings. Marketplace profiles need some human input.

onboarding.why: Scoping an unknown half-built codebase needs human judgement and a scoping call or quote.

delivery.why: Coding agents can do much of the work, but debugging, deployment, auth and payments need Ricardo's review. The work is project-based, and each project is different.

billing.why: Fixed-price milestones through a marketplace or Stripe.

support.why: Clients expect revisions and follow-ups, which needs human time.

scores.R_why: This fits Ricardo's technical skills and costs almost nothing to start. However, it is service work: it consumes his limited hours and is not agent-run with approval only.
scores.M_why: There is real demand now. However, the AI tools themselves are closing the gap, and many freelancers and agencies already offer 'vibe-code rescue' [E].
scores.one_line: A good skill fit and a cheap test, but it is a time-for-money service with shrinking headroom. Two sources from the same channel, with no claims.

acquisition.why: Local SEO, Google Maps, Meta ads and Facebook groups are legal. Local word of mouth and community presence are what drive success.

onboarding.why: Online signup, a fob/app access system and direct debit (e.g. GoCardless).

delivery.why: A physical facility needs cleaning, equipment maintenance, safety work and possibly classes or staff.

support.why: On-site issues, access faults and member complaints.

scores.R_why: A lease, fit-out and equipment cost tens to hundreds of thousands of pounds [E], with landlord commitments, insurance and staffing. Impossible on £300 and 6-8 h/week.
scores.M_why: Budget chains such as PureGym and The Gym Group dominate the UK, including around Bromley. Only niche or boutique formats have room.
scores.one_line: A capital-intensive physical venue completely outside Ricardo's constraints.

acquisition.why: Airbnb, Hipcamp, Canopy & Stars and Pitchup provide inbound demand, but the business is heavily dependent on these platforms.

onboarding.why: Platform booking and automated check-in messages.

delivery.why: Cleaning, linen changes, maintenance and guest issues need a local human or paid cleaners.

support.why: Agents can handle guest messaging; on-site problems need a person.

scores.R_why: Ricardo has no land, and land near London is expensive. Planning permission is needed (beyond the 28/60-day permitted-development allowance), plus setup capital, and the site would be far from Bromley. Not feasible on £300.
scores.M_why: UK glamping is popular but supply grew strongly after COVID. Occupancy is seasonal and pricing competition has increased.
scores.one_line: Platform-driven bookings automate well, but it needs land, planning and capital, and the claims are second-hand US figures. Not viable for Ricardo.

acquisition.why: Marketplaces (no UK Goldbelly equivalent; options include Amazon Fresh and Etsy limits), social reels and paid ads are inbound.

delivery.why: Food production, cold-chain packing and courier dispatch are physical and need a human every order.

support.why: Agents can triage, but warm-box refunds and food-safety complaints need judgement.

scores.R_why: It needs an existing food business, council food registration, cold-chain packaging and high UK courier costs. The sources are established restaurants or smokehouses, not starters.
scores.M_why: Specialist UK food DTC exists (e.g. Pipers Farm, smokehouses). The COVID demand spike has faded, and margins are thin after shipping.
scores.one_line: The first-hand claims come from existing producers, and the Goldbelly spike was COVID-specific. Physical food logistics make it unsuitable for an agent-run UK solo business.
